def: A careful study of something to understand it better.
ex: The analysis of last year's sales showed a clear drop in the spring.
nat: We need a deeper analysis before we make a decision.

mis.bad: We need to analysis the data first.
mis.good: We need to analyze the data first.
mis.why: The verb is analyze; analysis is the noun.

def: A reason or set of reasons given to support an idea, or a disagreement.
ex: Her argument for working four days a week convinced most of the team.
nat: They had a loud argument about who should pay the bill.

mis.bad: We had a discussion and he got angry, so it was a bad argument of ideas.
mis.good: We had an argument and he got angry.
mis.why: In English, argument often means a quarrel; use discussion for a calm talk.

def: A strong effect that something has on a person or situation.
ex: The new law had a huge impact on small businesses in the region.
nat: Social media has changed the impact of advertising.

mis.bad: The new rule had a big impact in our work.
mis.good: The new rule had a big impact on our work.
mis.why: Use the preposition "on" after impact.

def: Something you accept as true without proof.
ex: Your plan is based on the assumption that prices will stay the same.
nat: It is a common assumption, but it is not always correct.

mis.bad: I made a wrong assumption of him.
mis.good: I made a wrong assumption about him.
mis.why: Assumption is followed by "about" or "that", not "of".

def: A particular way of thinking about something.
ex: Living abroad gave me a new perspective on my own country.
nat: From my perspective, the meeting was a waste of time.

mis.bad: Under my perspective, the idea is bad.
mis.good: From my perspective, the idea is bad.
mis.why: Use "from" with perspective, not "under".

def: The way you understand or explain the meaning of something.
ex: Each reader has a different interpretation of the poem's last line.
nat: Your interpretation of the results seems too optimistic.

mis.bad: The interpreter of the poem is open to many readings.
mis.good: The interpretation of the poem is open to many readings.
mis.why: An interpreter is a person who translates speech; the idea of meaning is interpretation.

def: A statement that explains the exact meaning of a word or idea.
ex: The dictionary gives three different definitions of this rather difficult word.
nat: By my definition, a good friend always tells the truth.

mis.bad: What is the definition of this word means?
mis.good: What is the definition of this word?
mis.why: Do not add a second verb; "definition" is the noun for the meaning itself.

def: A basic structure of ideas or rules that you use to plan or understand something.
ex: The report provides a legal framework for protecting personal data online.
nat: We need a clear framework to evaluate new ideas.

mis.bad: The framework of the house was built with wood framework.
mis.good: The frame of the house was built with wood.
mis.why: Framework means a system of ideas or rules; for a physical structure use frame.

def: An idea about how something is or should be.
ex: The concept of free time is very new in some cultures.
nat: It is a simple concept, but hard to put into practice.

mis.bad: I did not understand the concept of that.
mis.good: I did not understand the concept.
mis.why: Do not add "of that" after concept; use "of + noun" or nothing.

def: The situation in which something happens, which helps you understand it.
ex: Without the right context, his joke sounded rude to the guests.
nat: You can often guess a word's meaning from the context.

mis.bad: In this context of that word, it means something else.
mis.good: In this context, the word means something else.
mis.why: Do not stack "of that word" after context; keep it simple.

def: The standards used to judge or decide something.
ex: The company uses strict criteria to choose which candidates to interview.
nat: These criteria are clear to everyone on the committee.

mis.bad: The criterias for this job are very strict.
mis.good: The criteria for this job are very strict.
mis.why: Criteria is already plural (singular: criterion); it does not take an extra -s.

def: One of several things that affect a result.
ex: Price is an important factor when people choose a new phone.
nat: Several factors led to the company's sudden success.

mis.bad: The price is a important factor.
mis.good: Price is an important factor.
mis.why: Use "an" before a vowel sound: an important factor.

def: One part or feature of a situation or idea.
ex: The most difficult aspect of the job is dealing with angry customers.
nat: We should look at every aspect of the problem.

mis.bad: Another aspect to consider it is the cost.
mis.good: Another aspect to consider is the cost.
mis.why: Do not add "it" as a second subject.

def: A basic rule or belief that guides how you act or think.
ex: He refused the bribe because it went against his principles.
nat: In principle, I agree with your idea, but I have doubts.

mis.bad: The principal of honesty is important to me.
mis.good: The principle of honesty is important to me.
mis.why: Principal means main or the head of a school; the rule or belief is principle.

def: A particular way of doing something.
ex: This method of learning words works better for me than flashcards.
nat: There are several methods for solving this kind of problem.

mis.bad: I use a good method to learn the English.
mis.good: I use a good method to learn English.
mis.why: Do not use "the" before a language name.

def: A series of actions that you take to achieve a result.
ex: The application process takes about two weeks from start to finish.
nat: Learning a language is a slow process.

mis.bad: I am in process to learn English.
mis.good: I am in the process of learning English.
mis.why: The correct phrase is "in the process of + -ing".

def: The way the parts of something are arranged or organized.
ex: The structure of the report makes it easy to follow.
nat: The company has a very flat structure with few managers.

mis.bad: The structure of the building is very structure.
mis.good: The structure of the building is very strong.
mis.why: Structure is a noun; do not use it as an adjective for strength.

def: The purpose of something, or what it does.
ex: The main function of this button is to save your work.
nat: A good manager has a clear function in the team.

mis.bad: The function of this machine is for cut paper.
mis.good: The function of this machine is to cut paper.
mis.why: After "function is", use "to + verb".

def: A subject or problem that people discuss or must deal with.
ex: Climate change is the most serious issue facing our generation.
nat: We had an issue with the payment, so I called the bank.

mis.bad: I have an issue to understand this rule.
mis.good: I have an issue understanding this rule.
mis.why: After "have an issue" use "with" or "-ing", not "to + verb".

def: A subject that you talk or write about.
ex: The topic of today's lecture in our history class is renewable energy.
nat: Let's change the topic; I do not want to talk about work.

mis.bad: Let's talk about a topic of that.
mis.good: Let's talk about that topic.
mis.why: Word order: that topic, not "a topic of that".

def: The main idea in a book, film, or event.
ex: Friendship is the central theme of the novel that we read last term.
nat: The party had a pirate theme, and everyone wore costumes.

mis.bad: The theme of the movie is about friendship.
mis.good: The theme of the movie is friendship.
mis.why: Do not add "about" after "the theme is".

def: A set of questions that you ask many people to learn their opinions.
ex: A recent survey found that most workers prefer flexible hours.
nat: The company sent a short survey to all of its customers.

mis.bad: I made a research with 100 students about it.
mis.good: I did a survey of 100 students about it.
mis.why: A set of questions to many people is a survey; research is uncountable and is not "made".

def: Careful study to discover new facts about a subject.
ex: Recent research suggests that sleep helps people remember new information.
nat: She does research on climate change at the university.

mis.bad: The researches show that coffee is healthy.
mis.good: Research shows that coffee is healthy.
mis.why: Research is uncountable: no plural "researches" and no "the" for general statements.

def: A final decision or opinion that you reach after thinking.
ex: After reading all the reports, we reached the conclusion that the project had failed.
nat: The conclusion of the article was surprising.

mis.bad: In conclusion that, I disagree.
mis.good: In conclusion, I disagree.
mis.why: Do not put "that" after "in conclusion"; use a comma.

def: A short description of the main points of something.
ex: Please write a short summary of the article for tomorrow.
nat: Here is a summary of what we discussed in the meeting.

mis.bad: I made a resume of the book.
mis.good: I wrote a summary of the book.
mis.why: Resume (without accents) means a CV in English; a short account of a book is a summary.

def: A group of different things of the same general type, or the limits between two points.
ex: The shop sells a wide range of products at low prices.
nat: The price range for these laptops is between 500 and 900 dollars.

mis.bad: The prices go from 10 until 50 dollars.
mis.good: The prices range from 10 to 50 dollars.
mis.why: Use "range from X to Y"; "until" is for time.

def: To guess the size, cost, or value of something using the information you have.
ex: Experts estimate that the new bridge will cost about fifty million dollars.
nat: We estimated the delay at two hours, but it took three.

mis.bad: I estimate to finish the work tomorrow.
mis.good: I estimate that I will finish the work tomorrow.
mis.why: Estimate is followed by "that + clause" or a noun, not by "to + verb".

def: The relationship between two numbers that shows how much bigger one is than the other.
ex: The ratio of students to teachers in this school is twenty to one.
nat: The ratio of boys to girls in the class is equal.

mis.bad: The ratio is of three to one.
mis.good: The ratio is three to one.
mis.why: Do not put "of" before the numbers after "is".

def: A part of a whole, or the relationship between the sizes of two things.
ex: A large proportion of the population in this country lives in big cities.
nat: The cost is out of proportion to the benefits.

mis.bad: A big proportion of people is unhappy.
mis.good: A big proportion of people are unhappy.
mis.why: The verb agrees with the noun after "of" (people), so it is plural.

def: The larger part of a group of people or things.
ex: The majority of voters supported the new plan in the election.
nat: Most of the time, the majority wins.

mis.bad: The majority of people is in favor.
mis.good: The majority of people are in favor.
mis.why: After "the majority of + plural noun", the verb is plural.

def: A smaller part of a group, or a group that is different from the main one.
ex: Only a small minority of employees disagreed with the new rule.
nat: Several ethnic minorities live in this part of the city.

mis.bad: I am in minority in this team.
mis.good: I am in the minority in this team.
mis.why: Use "the" in "in the minority".

def: A habit of behaving in a certain way.
ex: He has a tendency to talk too fast when he is nervous.
nat: There is a tendency to overestimate how long tasks take.

mis.bad: He has a tendency of arrive late.
mis.good: He has a tendency to arrive late.
mis.why: Use "tendency to + verb".

def: Something that exists or happens, especially something unusual that is interesting to study.
ex: Northern lights are a natural phenomenon that attracts many tourists.
nat: Remote work is a global phenomenon, not just a local trend.

mis.bad: There are many strange phenomenons in nature.
mis.good: There are many strange phenomena in nature.
mis.why: The plural of phenomenon is phenomena.

def: A regular way in which something happens or is done.
ex: Scientists noticed a pattern in the way the birds moved each winter.
nat: My sleep pattern has changed since I started working nights.

mis.bad: I follow the same pattern of always.
mis.good: I follow the same pattern every time.
mis.why: "Of always" is not correct; use "every time".

def: To say that something is true, often without proof.
ex: The company claims that its new phone has the best battery on the market.
nat: Nobody could claim that the test was easy.

mis.bad: The company claimed to me that I should pay.
mis.good: The company told me that I should pay.
mis.why: Claim does not take an indirect object like "claim to me"; use tell.

def: The process of thinking about something in a logical way.
ex: I did not follow her reasoning, so I asked her to explain.
nat: Good reasoning skills are important in this job.

mis.bad: I did not understand his reasoning of the problem.
mis.good: I did not understand his reasoning about the problem.
mis.why: Use "reasoning about" or "behind", not "of the problem".

def: A way of thinking that follows clear and sensible rules.
ex: There is no logic in spending money on something you never use.
nat: Her argument has a certain logic that is hard to deny.

mis.bad: It has no logical in this idea.
mis.good: There is no logic in this idea.
mis.why: Logical is an adjective; the noun is logic.

def: Based on good reasons, or officially acceptable.
ex: You can only enter the country with a valid passport.
nat: That is a valid point, and we should think about it.

mis.bad: My passport is valid until to June.
mis.good: My passport is valid until June.
mis.why: Do not combine "until" and "to".

def: Connected to the subject that you are talking about.
ex: Only include information that is relevant to the topic of your essay.
nat: Your experience is highly relevant to this job.

mis.bad: This information is relevant with the topic.
mis.good: This information is relevant to the topic.
mis.why: Relevant is followed by "to".

def: Based on facts and not influenced by personal feelings.
ex: A judge should be objective and listen to both sides of the story.
nat: It is hard to stay objective when family is involved.

mis.bad: I want to be objective of my work.
mis.good: It is hard to be objective about your own work.
mis.why: Use "objective about" and keep one clear adjective.

def: Based on personal feelings or opinions rather than facts.
ex: Taste in music is very subjective, so we should not argue about it.
nat: That is a subjective opinion, not a fact.

mis.bad: It is a subjective of opinion.
mis.good: It is a subjective opinion.
mis.why: Subjective is an adjective placed before the noun; no "of".

def: Always behaving or happening in the same way.
ex: She has been consistent in her work, so her results are always good.
nat: The results are consistent with our earlier tests.

mis.bad: Your results are consistent of our tests.
mis.good: Your results are consistent with our tests.
mis.why: Consistent is followed by "with".

def: To say the opposite of what someone else has said, or to be different from another statement.
ex: The new data contradicts everything that the earlier study found.
nat: Please do not contradict me in front of the customers.

mis.bad: The results contradict with the first study.
mis.good: The results contradict the first study.
mis.why: Contradict is a transitive verb; do not use "with".

def: To show clearly that something is true or how something works.
ex: The study demonstrates that regular exercise improves memory in older adults.
nat: The sales manager demonstrated how the new software works.

mis.bad: The teacher demonstrated us how to do it.
mis.good: The teacher showed us how to do it.
mis.why: Demonstrate does not take an indirect object; use show someone how.

def: To show that something exists or is likely to be true.
ex: Recent figures indicate that the economy is growing more slowly than expected.
nat: The arrow indicates the direction of the nearest exit.

mis.bad: The report indicates to a problem.
mis.good: The report indicates a problem.
mis.why: Indicate is a transitive verb and takes no preposition here.

def: To offer an idea or plan for someone to consider, or to show that something may be true.
ex: I suggest that we meet at nine instead of ten tomorrow.
nat: The evidence suggests that the system was not working properly.

mis.bad: I suggest you to go home early.
mis.good: I suggest that you go home early.
mis.why: Suggest is not followed by "someone to + verb"; use "that" clause or -ing.

def: To make something known that was secret or hidden.
ex: The investigation revealed that the company had hidden its losses for years.
nat: She did not want to reveal the name of her new employer.

mis.bad: The company revealed to me the secrets of it.
mis.good: The company revealed its secrets to me.
mis.why: Word order: reveal the thing, then "to" the person.

def: To make something clear by giving examples or showing pictures.
ex: The teacher drew a graph to illustrate how prices change over time.
nat: This story illustrates the importance of planning ahead.

mis.bad: The example illustrate well the idea.
mis.good: The example illustrates the idea well.
mis.why: Third-person singular needs -s and the adverb goes after the object.

def: To decide how good, useful, or successful something is.
ex: The committee will evaluate each proposal before announcing the winner.
nat: The company evaluates its employees once a year.

mis.bad: The teacher will evaluate us on Friday for the exam.
mis.good: The teacher will evaluate our work on Friday.
mis.why: One evaluates a thing or performance; do not leave the object vague.

def: To look at something carefully to learn more about it.
ex: The doctor examined my knee and said I should rest for a week.
nat: The report examines the causes of the economic crisis.

mis.bad: I examined the answer to the examination yesterday.
mis.good: I examined the document carefully.
mis.why: Keep verb and noun apart: examine is a verb, examination is a noun.

def: To try to find out the facts about something such as a crime or accident.
ex: Police are investigating the cause of the fire at the old factory.
nat: The company hired a team to investigate the problem.

mis.bad: The police investigated about the accident.
mis.good: The police investigated the accident.
mis.why: Investigate is transitive and takes no preposition.

def: To look at things to see how they are similar or different.
ex: Before you buy a phone, compare prices in at least three stores.
nat: Compared with last year, sales have gone up by ten percent.

mis.bad: Compared of last year, sales are higher.
mis.good: Compared with last year, sales are higher.
mis.why: Use "compared with" or "compared to".

def: A clear difference between two things when you compare them.
ex: There is a sharp contrast between the rich and poor parts of the city.
nat: In contrast to my sister, I love getting up early.

mis.bad: In contrast of him, I am shy.
mis.good: In contrast to him, I am shy.
mis.why: Use "in contrast to" with a person or thing.

def: To see or understand the difference between two things.
ex: It is hard to distinguish between the twins because they look so alike.
nat: Can you distinguish real news from fake news online?

mis.bad: I cannot distinguish one of the other.
mis.good: I cannot distinguish one from the other.
mis.why: Use "distinguish X from Y".

def: To recognize someone or something and say who or what they are.
ex: Engineers identified the problem within an hour and fixed it quickly.
nat: Can you identify the man in this photograph?

mis.bad: I identify me with the main character.
mis.good: I identify with the main character.
mis.why: "Identify with" has no reflexive pronoun.

def: To find out or decide something after careful thought or study.
ex: Tests will determine whether the water is safe to drink.
nat: Your score will determine which class you join.

mis.bad: The doctor determined to me the cause.
mis.good: The doctor determined the cause.
mis.why: Determine does not take an indirect object with "to".

def: To start something that will last, or to prove that something is true.
ex: Her grandfather established the company in 1950 with only three employees.
nat: The police have not yet established the cause of the crash.

mis.bad: He established a company in the 1990.
mis.good: He established a company in the 1990s.
mis.why: Decades take "the 1990s", with a final -s.

def: To get something from a particular source.
ex: Many English words are derived from Latin and French, so they look familiar.
nat: She derives great satisfaction from helping other people.

mis.bad: This word derives of Latin.
mis.good: This word derives from Latin.
mis.why: Derive is followed by "from".

def: To include something or someone as a necessary part.
ex: The job involves traveling to other countries at least twice a month.
nat: I do not want to get involved in their argument.

mis.bad: The job involves to travel a lot.
mis.good: The job involves traveling a lot.
mis.why: Involve is followed by -ing, not "to + verb".

def: To show or be a sign of something, or to think carefully.
ex: The test results reflect how hard the students worked this year.
nat: After the accident, he reflected on what was truly important.

mis.bad: The prices reflects the quality.
mis.good: The prices reflect the quality.
mis.why: Plural subject needs the verb without -s.

def: To speak or act officially for someone, or to be a symbol or example of something.
ex: The lawyer will represent him in court next week at nine o'clock.
nat: The red line on the map represents the main road.

mis.bad: The lawyer will represent to him in court.
mis.good: The lawyer will represent him in court.
mis.why: Represent is transitive; no "to".

def: To make something stronger or more certain.
ex: The new data reinforces our belief that the plan will succeed.
nat: Engineers reinforced the bridge with steel after the storm.

mis.bad: The teacher reinforced to the students the rule.
mis.good: The teacher reinforced the rule for the students.
mis.why: Reinforce takes the thing as direct object.

def: Something difficult that tests your ability.
ex: Learning to code was a big challenge, but I enjoyed it.
nat: We face a new challenge every day in this job.

mis.bad: It is a challenge for to learn Chinese.
mis.good: It is a challenge to learn Chinese.
mis.why: Do not add "for" before "to + verb".

def: To deal with a problem or question.
ex: The manager promised to address the complaints before the end of the week.
nat: We need to address this problem as soon as possible.

mis.bad: We must address to this problem soon.
mis.good: We must address this problem soon.
mis.why: Address is transitive and takes no preposition.

def: To make something easy to notice so that people pay attention to it.
ex: The report highlights the need for better training in all departments.
nat: I highlighted the main points in yellow before the exam.

mis.bad: The report highlights about the problem.
mis.good: The report highlights the problem.
mis.why: Highlight is transitive; no "about".

def: To describe the main points of something without giving all the details.
ex: The director outlined her plans for the new office in a short speech.
nat: Let me outline the main steps of the process first.

mis.bad: She outlined me her plans.
mis.good: She outlined her plans to me.
mis.why: Outline does not take an indirect object directly.

def: A short description of the main features of something.
ex: The first chapter gives a brief overview of the history of the city.
nat: I only need a quick overview, not every detail.

mis.bad: I will make an overview for you.
mis.good: I will give you an overview.
mis.why: Collocation: give or provide an overview.

def: A clear understanding of the true nature of something.
ex: The interview gave me valuable insight into how the company really works.
nat: She offered an insight that nobody had thought about before.

mis.bad: The book gave me many insights of this subject.
mis.good: The book gave me many insights into this subject.
mis.why: Use "insight into".

def: A possible effect or result of an action or decision.
ex: The new law has serious implications for small business owners.
nat: I do not like the implication that I was lying.

mis.bad: The decision has big implications to us.
mis.good: The decision has big implications for us.
mis.why: Implication is followed by "for".

def: A rule or condition that limits what you can do, or a weakness.
ex: The software has some limitations, but it is good enough for beginners.
nat: There is no limitation on the number of guests.

mis.bad: I know my limitation to speak fast.
mis.good: I know my limitation: I cannot speak fast.
mis.why: Do not use "limitation to + verb"; rephrase with a colon or a clause.

def: The ability to develop or succeed in the future.
ex: This young player has great potential and could become a star.
nat: The city has the potential to become a major tourist center.

mis.bad: She has a big potential of success.
mis.good: She has great potential for success.
mis.why: Potential is usually uncountable here, and takes "for" or "to".

def: The importance or meaning of something.
ex: Historians still discuss the significance of this ancient discovery in their books.
nat: The date has no special significance for us.

mis.bad: The significance of the word is not significance.
mis.good: The significance of the word is not clear.
mis.why: Do not repeat the noun as an adjective; use "clear".

def: To say or write something clearly and formally.
ex: The report states that the factory must close by the end of March.
nat: Please state your name and address clearly for the record.

mis.bad: He stated me that he was tired.
mis.good: He told me that he was tired.
mis.why: State does not take an indirect object; use tell.

def: To agree that something is true, usually when you do not want to.
ex: He finally admitted that he had made a serious mistake.
nat: I must admit that I did not read the whole book.

mis.bad: He admitted to me that he is lost.
mis.good: He admitted to me that he was lost.
mis.why: In reported speech, the verb tense usually shifts back to the past.

def: To say that something is not true.
ex: The minister denied that he had received money from the company.
nat: She cannot deny that she was at the party.

mis.bad: He denied to have taken the money.
mis.good: He denied taking the money.
mis.why: Deny is followed by -ing or a noun, not by "to + verb".

def: To tell someone about a possible danger or problem.
ex: The doctor warned me that I should stop eating so much sugar.
nat: I warned him not to touch the hot oven.

mis.bad: The doctor warned that I stop eating sugar.
mis.good: The doctor warned me to stop eating sugar.
mis.why: Use "warn someone to do something" or "warn someone that".

def: To keep saying that something is true, or to keep something in good condition.
ex: She maintains that she was at home with her family all evening.
nat: The company must maintain its equipment to keep workers safe.

mis.bad: I maintain that she to be innocent.
mis.good: I maintain that she is innocent.
mis.why: After maintain that, use a full clause with a conjugated verb.

def: To accept that something is true or exists.
ex: The manager acknowledged that the team had been working under heavy pressure.
nat: He never acknowledged my email, so I wrote to him again.

mis.bad: I acknowledge to him the receipt.
mis.good: I acknowledged his email.
mis.why: Acknowledge takes the thing directly: acknowledge an email.

def: To say something briefly without giving many details.
ex: She mentioned that she might be late, but she did not say why.
nat: Did I mention that I am moving to Canada next month?

mis.bad: She mentioned me about the party.
mis.good: She mentioned the party to me.
mis.why: Mention does not take "someone about"; use "mention something to someone".

def: To tell people something officially or publicly.
ex: The company announced that it will open three new stores next year.
nat: They announced the winner at the end of the ceremony.

mis.bad: They announced me the results.
mis.good: They announced the results to me.
mis.why: Announce does not take an indirect object directly.

def: To say that you are unhappy about something.
ex: Several customers complained to the manager that the service was too slow.
nat: My neighbor always complains about the noise from my music.

mis.bad: He complained the noise to the manager.
mis.good: He complained to the manager about the noise.
mis.why: Complain needs "about" for the thing and "to" for the person.

def: To suggest a plan or idea for people to consider.
ex: The mayor proposed a new tax on cars that pollute the air.
nat: I propose that we take a short break before the next topic.

mis.bad: I propose you to take a break.
mis.good: I propose that you take a break.
mis.why: Propose is followed by a "that" clause, not "someone to + verb".

def: To say that something is good or suggest that someone should do it.
ex: My doctor recommended that I drink more water during the day.
nat: Can you recommend a good restaurant near the station?

mis.bad: I recommend you to visit the museum.
mis.good: I recommend that you visit the museum.
mis.why: Recommend is usually followed by a "that" clause or -ing, not "you to".

def: To say what you think will happen in the future.
ex: Experts predict that prices will keep rising for the rest of the year.
nat: It is hard to predict how people will react to the news.

mis.bad: Experts predict to rise the prices.
mis.good: Experts predict that prices will rise.
mis.why: Predict is followed by a noun or "that" clause.

def: To state something officially or in a firm way.
ex: The government declared a state of emergency after the floods.
nat: You must declare any money that you bring into the country.

mis.bad: I declared to the customs that I have nothing.
mis.good: I told the customs officer that I had nothing to declare.
mis.why: Declare is for formal statements; do not use "declare to" like "say to".

def: Used to say that something seems true based on what you have heard.
ex: Apparently, the flight was canceled because of the storm in Chicago.
nat: He is apparently sick, because he did not come to work.

mis.bad: Apparently the student is very apparently smart.
mis.good: Apparently, the student is very smart.
mis.why: Do not repeat the adverb; use it once at the start.

def: Used to say that you think something is probably true.
ex: Presumably, he missed the train, because he is usually very punctual.
nat: You are presumably tired after such a long flight.

mis.bad: Presumably he will to come tomorrow.
mis.good: Presumably he will come tomorrow.
mis.why: After "will", use the base verb without "to".

def: Used to say that something is believed to be true, but you doubt it.
ex: The restaurant is supposedly the best in town, but the food was cold.
nat: He supposedly lives in London, though nobody has seen him there.

mis.bad: Supposedly the pizza is a good, but I do not think so.
mis.good: Supposedly the pizza is good, but I do not think so.
mis.why: Do not add the article "a" before an adjective alone.

def: Used when you can give reasons to support a statement, although other people may disagree.
ex: Brazil is arguably the best football country in the world.
nat: This is arguably the most important election in years.

mis.bad: He is arguably be the best player.
mis.good: He is arguably the best player.
mis.why: Arguably goes before the phrase it modifies and does not combine with "be".

def: Used to say that something was said or reported, but it may not be true.
ex: The singer is reportedly planning to leave the band next year.
nat: Three people were reportedly injured in the accident.

mis.bad: It reportedly that he left.
mis.good: He has reportedly left.
mis.why: Reportedly is an adverb and needs a subject and verb in the sentence.

def: Used to show that a number or amount is not exact.
ex: The trip to the airport takes roughly forty minutes without traffic.
nat: There were roughly two hundred people at the meeting.

mis.bad: It takes roughly of forty minutes.
mis.good: It takes roughly forty minutes.
mis.why: Do not add "of" after roughly.

def: Used when a number or amount is close to the exact one.
ex: The flight lasts approximately ten hours, including a short stop.
nat: The repair will cost approximately three hundred dollars.

mis.bad: It costs approximately about ten dollars.
mis.good: It costs approximately ten dollars.
mis.why: Approximately already means "about"; do not use both.

def: To a small degree.
ex: I was somewhat surprised to see her at the party.
nat: The test was somewhat harder than I expected.

mis.bad: I am somewhat very tired.
mis.good: I am somewhat tired.
mis.why: Somewhat means "a little"; do not combine it with "very".

def: To a reasonable degree, but not very.
ex: The movie was fairly good, but I expected something better.
nat: She speaks English fairly well after only one year.

mis.bad: The test was fairly difficult, extremely.
mis.good: The test was fairly difficult.
mis.why: Do not add "extremely" after a "fairly" phrase; they contradict each other.

def: When compared with other things of the same kind.
ex: The rent in this area is relatively cheap compared with the city center.
nat: The job is relatively easy once you learn the system.

mis.bad: The price is relative cheap.
mis.good: The price is relatively cheap.
mis.why: Use the adverb relatively before an adjective.

def: Almost, but not completely.
ex: The old factory has been virtually empty since the company moved away.
nat: It is virtually impossible to find parking here on Saturdays.

mis.bad: The room is virtual empty.
mis.good: The room is virtually empty.
mis.why: Use the adverb virtually, not the adjective virtual.

def: Used to talk about the most important or basic part of something.
ex: The two products are essentially the same, but one costs more.
nat: Essentially, the project failed because we ran out of money.

mis.bad: The two products are essential the same.
mis.good: The two products are essentially the same.
mis.why: Use the adverb essentially to modify "the same".

def: Used to say what is most important when you simplify something.
ex: Basically, you just need to press the green button to start.
nat: The two phones are basically the same, except for the color.

mis.bad: Basically, the phone is basicly the same.
mis.good: Basically, the two phones are the same.
mis.why: Basically has no "ly" error; spell it basically and use it once.

def: In most cases or for most people.
ex: Generally, people in this city are friendly and helpful to visitors.
nat: The shops generally open at nine and close at six.

mis.bad: General, people are friendly here.
mis.good: Generally, people are friendly here.
mis.why: Use the adverb generally to start a sentence.

def: Used to say that something happens in the usual way.
ex: A typical day for me typically starts with a quick cup of coffee.
nat: Dinner in Spain typically starts after nine at night.

mis.bad: Typical, the meeting starts at nine.
mis.good: Typically, the meeting starts at nine.
mis.why: Use the adverb typically to modify a sentence.

def: Probably going to happen or be true.
ex: It is likely that the meeting will be moved to next week.
nat: She is likely to win the race because she trains every day.

mis.bad: It is probably that she will win.
mis.good: It is likely that she will win.
mis.why: Probably is an adverb; after "it is" use the adjective likely.

def: Not expected to happen or to be true.
ex: It is unlikely that the train will arrive on time in this snow.
nat: He is unlikely to change his mind about the plan.

mis.bad: It is not unlikely that he will not come.
mis.good: It is unlikely that he will come.
mis.why: Avoid the double negative; "unlikely" already means not likely.

def: To see or become aware of something.
ex: I did not notice that the shop had closed until I got there.
nat: Did you notice that she changed her hair color?

mis.bad: I noticed him to leave.
mis.good: I noticed him leaving.
mis.why: After notice + object, use -ing or the bare verb, not "to + verb".

def: To make someone remember something.
ex: Please remind me to call the dentist before the office closes.
nat: This song reminds me of my school days.

mis.bad: The song reminds me my school days.
mis.good: The song reminds me of my school days.
mis.why: Use "remind someone of something".

def: To have earned something because of how you behave or what you do.
ex: After working so hard all year, you deserve a long holiday.
nat: Everyone deserves a second chance, in my opinion.

mis.bad: You deserve to be rewarded of your work.
mis.good: You deserve to be rewarded for your work.
mis.why: Use "reward for", not "reward of".

def: To say that you will not do or accept something.
ex: She refused to answer any questions about her private life.
nat: The bank refused my request for a loan.

mis.bad: He refused to me the loan.
mis.good: He refused me the loan.
mis.why: Use "refuse someone something" without "to me".

def: To feel sorry about something that you did or did not do.
ex: I really regret not studying more when I was a younger student.
nat: We regret to inform you that your application was not successful.

mis.bad: I regret to not have studied more.
mis.good: I regret not studying more.
mis.why: To talk about a past action you feel sorry for, use "regret + -ing".

def: To stay away from something or prevent it from happening.
ex: Try to avoid driving in the city center during rush hour.
nat: He avoids eating sugar because he is trying to lose weight.

mis.bad: I avoid to eat sugar.
mis.good: I avoid eating sugar.
mis.why: Avoid is followed by -ing, not "to + verb".

def: To pay no attention to something or someone.
ex: He ignored the warning signs and kept driving through the storm.
nat: You cannot ignore a problem like this for very long.

mis.bad: I ignore how to fix this.
mis.good: I do not know how to fix this.
mis.why: Ignore means pay no attention to; it does not mean "not know" (false friend of "ignorar").

def: To change something slightly so that it works better.
ex: You can adjust the height of the chair with this small lever.
nat: It takes time to adjust to life in a new country.

mis.bad: Please adjust the volume of the music down.
mis.good: Please turn the volume down.
mis.why: Adjust means change slightly; use "turn down" for volume.

def: To ask formally for a job, place, or permission, or to use something in a situation.
ex: I applied for three jobs last week and got two interviews.
nat: This rule only applies to students who are under eighteen.

mis.bad: I applied to the job in your company.
mis.good: I applied for the job in your company.
mis.why: Apply for a job, apply to a company.

def: To plan or organize something in advance.
ex: I arranged a meeting with the client for Tuesday morning.
nat: Can you arrange a taxi to the airport for six?

mis.bad: I arranged him to come at six.
mis.good: I arranged for him to come at six.
mis.why: Use "arrange for someone to do something".

def: To fix or join one thing to another.
ex: I attached the report to this email so you can read it.
nat: He attached a note to the box before he left.

mis.bad: I attached the file in the email.
mis.good: I attached the file to the email.
mis.why: Use "attach something to something".

def: To make people interested or draw them to a place.
ex: The festival attracts thousands of visitors from all over the world.
nat: Bright colors attract insects, so wear white at night.

mis.bad: The festival attracts to many tourists.
mis.good: The festival attracts many tourists.
mis.why: Attract is transitive and takes no preposition.

def: To be the property of someone, or to be part of a group.
ex: This book belongs to my sister, so please give it back to her.
nat: I feel that I belong in this team.

mis.bad: This book belongs for my sister.
mis.good: This book belongs to my sister.
mis.why: Belong is followed by "to" for ownership.

def: To say that someone or something caused a problem.
ex: Do not blame yourself; the accident was not your fault.
nat: Many people blame social media for rising stress levels.

mis.bad: They blamed the delay of the weather.
mis.good: They blamed the weather for the delay.
mis.why: Use "blame someone or something for something".

def: Knowing that something exists or is true.
ex: I was not aware that the office closes early on Fridays.
nat: Are you aware of the risks involved in this plan?

mis.bad: I am aware about the problem.
mis.good: I am aware of the problem.
mis.why: Aware is followed by "of".

def: Well known to you, or easy to recognize.
ex: Your face looks very familiar to me; have we met somewhere before?
nat: Are you familiar with this software?

mis.bad: I am not familiar to this software.
mis.good: I am not familiar with this software.
mis.why: Use "familiar with" when you know something.

def: Easy to see or understand.
ex: It was obvious that she was tired after the long trip.
nat: The answer seems obvious, but it is not.

mis.bad: It is obviously that he is lying.
mis.good: It is obvious that he is lying.
mis.why: After "it is", use the adjective obvious, not the adverb.

def: Right for a particular purpose or person.
ex: This hotel is not suitable for families with small children.
nat: I am looking for a suitable place to hold the meeting.

mis.bad: This job is suitable to me.
mis.good: This job is suitable for me.
mis.why: Use "suitable for".

def: Difficult to deal with, or strong enough to survive hard conditions.
ex: It was a tough decision, but we chose to move abroad.
nat: The meat was so tough that I could not cut it.

mis.bad: The exam was very toughy.
mis.good: The exam was very tough.
mis.why: The spelling and form is tough; there is no "toughy".

def: Almost, but not completely.
ex: I nearly missed the bus because I woke up late.
nat: It took nearly three hours to drive to the coast.

mis.bad: I nearly not missed the bus.
mis.good: I nearly missed the bus.
mis.why: Nearly already has a near-negative meaning; do not add "not".

def: In most cases, or mainly.
ex: The audience was mostly young people from the local university.
nat: I mostly work from home, but I go to the office on Fridays.

mis.bad: I mostly of the time stay home.
mis.good: I mostly stay at home.
mis.why: Mostly cannot be used with "of the time"; use "most of the time" or just mostly.

def: Almost not.
ex: I could hardly hear the speaker because the room was so noisy.
nat: There is hardly any milk left in the fridge.

mis.bad: I hardly never go to the gym.
mis.good: I hardly ever go to the gym.
mis.why: Hardly is already negative; say "hardly ever", not "hardly never".

def: Only just; almost not.
ex: I barely had time to eat lunch before the meeting started.
nat: She was so tired that she could barely stand.

mis.bad: I barely did not see him.
mis.good: I barely saw him.
mis.why: Barely is already negative; do not add "not".

def: At the present time.
ex: The company is currently looking for a new marketing manager.
nat: I am currently living with my parents.

mis.bad: Actually I am living in Lisbon.
mis.good: Currently I am living in Lisbon.
mis.why: Actually means "in fact", not "at present" (false friend of "atualmente").

def: At the present time, compared with the past.
ex: Nowadays, most people use their phones to pay for coffee.
nat: Prices are much higher nowadays than they were ten years ago.

mis.bad: Nowadays I used to go to the gym.
mis.good: Nowadays I go to the gym.
mis.why: Used to refers to the past; do not use it with nowadays.

def: Many times or very often.
ex: Customers frequently ask about the return policy during the sale.
nat: He travels frequently for work, so he is rarely home.

mis.bad: He frequently is late for work.
mis.good: He is frequently late for work.
mis.why: Frequency adverbs go after "be" but before most other verbs.

def: Not often.
ex: We rarely eat out because cooking at home is cheaper.
nat: He rarely speaks in meetings, but his ideas are good.

mis.bad: I rarely don't go to the gym.
mis.good: I rarely go to the gym.
mis.why: Rarely is already negative; do not add "don't".

def: Without any delay.
ex: Please call me immediately if you have any problem with the system.
nat: He answered the question immediately, without any hesitation.

mis.bad: I will do it immediate.
mis.good: I will do it immediately.
mis.why: Use the adverb immediately after the verb phrase.

def: In an easy way, or only.
ex: The recipe is simply a mix of eggs, flour, and milk.
nat: I simply did not have enough time to finish.

mis.bad: I simple forgot my key.
mis.good: I simply forgot my key.
mis.why: Use the adverb simply to modify a verb.

def: Used to show that something is more true for one case than for others.
ex: I love all kinds of fruit, especially mangoes and fresh strawberries.
nat: It is cold here, especially in the early morning.

mis.bad: I like all sports, specially football.
mis.good: I like all sports, especially football.
mis.why: Especially is used to emphasize; "specially" means "for a special purpose".

def: To a very high degree.
ex: The test was extremely difficult, and only a few people passed.
nat: I am extremely grateful for your help with the project.

mis.bad: The movie was extremely very good.
mis.good: The movie was extremely good.
mis.why: Do not combine "extremely" with "very".

def: A situation in which you do not have enough of something.
ex: A lack of sleep can make it hard to concentrate at work.
nat: The project failed because of a lack of money.

mis.bad: The lack of money is the reason of failure.
mis.good: The lack of money is the reason for the failure.
mis.why: Use "reason for".

def: To get something useful, such as experience or an advantage.
ex: I gained a lot of experience during my first year at the company.
nat: Many people gain weight during the winter months.

mis.bad: I gained a good grade in the test.
mis.good: I got a good grade on the test.
mis.why: Gain is not used for grades; use get.

def: To make something smaller in size, amount, or price.
ex: The company reduced prices by twenty percent to attract more customers.
nat: Exercise can reduce stress and help you sleep better.

mis.bad: The company reduced to the prices.
mis.good: The company reduced the prices.
mis.why: Reduce is transitive and takes no "to" here.

def: To become or make something larger in amount or number.
ex: The number of online shoppers has increased sharply in recent years.
nat: We need to increase our sales by ten percent this year.

mis.bad: Sales increased in ten percent.
mis.good: Sales increased by ten percent.
mis.why: Use "by" for the amount of change.

def: To become larger or make something larger.
ex: The company plans to expand into three new countries next year.
nat: We want to expand our vocabulary before the exam.

mis.bad: The company wants to expand to the market.
mis.good: The company wants to expand into the market.
mis.why: Expand into a market, not "to the market".

def: To change often, going up and down.
ex: Prices of fresh vegetables fluctuate depending on the season and the weather.
nat: My mood fluctuates a lot when I am stressed.

mis.bad: The prices fluctuates every week.
mis.good: The prices fluctuate every week.
mis.why: Plural subject needs a verb without -s.

def: To become smaller, weaker, or less; or to politely refuse.
ex: Newspaper sales have declined steadily since the rise of the internet.
nat: She politely declined the invitation because she was busy.

mis.bad: The sales declined in 20 percent.
mis.good: The sales declined by 20 percent.
mis.why: Use "by" for the amount of change.

def: To succeed in doing something difficult, or to be in charge of something.
ex: Somehow, I managed to finish the report before the deadline.
nat: She manages a team of ten people in the sales department.

mis.bad: I managed finish the report before the deadline.
mis.good: I managed to finish the report before the deadline.
mis.why: Manage is followed by "to + verb".

def: To try very hard to do something difficult.
ex: Many students struggle with grammar when they first start learning English.
nat: He struggled to stay awake during the long meeting.

mis.bad: He struggles to understand of the lesson.
mis.good: He struggles to understand the lesson.
mis.why: Do not add "of" after "understand".

def: To be likely to behave in a certain way.
ex: Young people tend to spend more time online than older adults.
nat: He tends to forget names, so he writes them down.

mis.bad: People tends to forget names.
mis.good: People tend to forget names.
mis.why: Plural subject needs the base verb without -s.

def: Slow to act or speak because you are not sure.
ex: She seemed hesitant about taking the job in another city.
nat: He gave a hesitant answer because he was not sure.

mis.bad: He was hesitant of accepting the offer.
mis.good: He was hesitant about accepting the offer.
mis.why: Use "hesitant about" or "hesitant to".

def: Very interested and excited about something that will happen.
ex: The children were eager to open their presents on Christmas morning.
nat: She is eager to learn and always asks good questions.

mis.bad: He is eager of learning new things.
mis.good: He is eager to learn new things.
mis.why: Use "eager to + verb".

def: Real and true, not false.
ex: She showed genuine interest in the project and asked many questions.
nat: These shoes are made of genuine leather, not plastic.

mis.bad: His interest is genuinely and strong.
mis.good: His interest is genuine and strong.
mis.why: Use the adjective genuine after "is"; genuinely is an adverb.

def: Very serious or bad.
ex: The storm caused severe damage to hundreds of homes in the area.
nat: She suffers from severe headaches, so she sees a doctor often.

mis.bad: The pain was too severe to bear it.
mis.good: The pain was too severe to bear.
mis.why: Do not repeat the object "it" after "bear".

def: Large in amount or importance.
ex: The company made a substantial profit despite the difficult year.
nat: There is substantial evidence that the new method works.

mis.bad: The profit was substantially.
mis.good: The profit was substantial.
mis.why: After "was", use the adjective substantial.

def: As much as you need.
ex: Do we have sufficient money to pay for the whole trip?
nat: Eight hours of sleep is usually sufficient for most adults.

mis.bad: We have sufficient of money.
mis.good: We have sufficient money.
mis.why: Do not use "of" after sufficient before an uncountable noun.

def: Good enough for a particular purpose.
ex: The hotel was cheap but adequate for a one-night stay.
nat: Make sure you get adequate sleep before the exam.

mis.bad: The room is adequate to the family.
mis.good: The room is adequate for the family.
mis.why: Use "adequate for".

def: Having more than one possible meaning.
ex: The instructions were ambiguous, so each person understood them differently.
nat: His answer was ambiguous, and nobody knew what he wanted.

mis.bad: The sentence is ambiguously unclear.
mis.good: The sentence is ambiguous.
mis.why: Do not combine ambiguously and unclear; use one adjective.

def: Easy to see or understand.
ex: It soon became apparent that the plan was not going to work.
nat: The reason for his anger was not apparent to anyone.

mis.bad: It became apparently that the plan failed.
mis.good: It became apparent that the plan failed.
mis.why: After "became", use the adjective apparent.

def: Having a good effect.
ex: Regular exercise is beneficial for both your body and your mind.
nat: The new rules will be beneficial to small companies.

mis.bad: Exercise is beneficial to health body.
mis.good: Exercise is beneficial to the body.
mis.why: "Health body" is wrong; use "the body" or "your health".

def: Having many parts and difficult to understand.
ex: The tax system in this country is too complex for most people.
nat: It is a complex problem with no simple solution.

mis.bad: The system is very complexed.
mis.good: The system is very complex.
mis.why: Complex is already an adjective; it has no -ed form.

def: Extremely important and necessary for success.
ex: Good communication is crucial for the success of any team.
nat: It is crucial that everyone arrives on time tomorrow.

mis.bad: Good communication is crucial to be successful.
mis.good: Good communication is crucial for success.
mis.why: Use "crucial for + noun".

def: Absolutely necessary.
ex: Water is essential for all forms of life on Earth.
nat: It is essential to back up your files every week.

mis.bad: Water is essential of life.
mis.good: Water is essential for life.
mis.why: Use "essential for".

def: Basic and very important.
ex: There is a fundamental difference between knowing a word and using it.
nat: Honesty is fundamental to any good relationship.

mis.bad: Honesty is fundamental of any good relationship.
mis.good: Honesty is fundamental to any good relationship.
mis.why: Use "fundamental to".

def: Useful and sensible in real situations.
ex: This course gives practical advice that you can use at work.
nat: She is a very practical person who always finds simple solutions.

mis.bad: It is a practic idea.
mis.good: It is a practical idea.
mis.why: The adjective is practical, with "-al".

def: Existing or happening in many places or among many people.
ex: There is widespread concern about the rising cost of living.
nat: The use of smartphones is now widespread in every country.

mis.bad: The problem is widespreaded in this city.
mis.good: The problem is widespread in this city.
mis.why: Widespread has no -ed form.

def: Unusual or surprising in a way that makes people notice.
ex: She made remarkable progress in English after only six months of study.
nat: It is remarkable that nobody was hurt in the accident.

mis.bad: It was a remark progress.
mis.good: It was remarkable progress.
mis.why: The adjective is remarkable; remark is a noun or verb.

def: Advanced and complex, or having a lot of experience and good taste.
ex: The hackers used a sophisticated method that the system could not detect.
nat: She has sophisticated taste in music and art.

mis.bad: The system is very sophisticate.
mis.good: The system is very sophisticated.
mis.why: The adjective ends with "-ed": sophisticated.

def: Not important or serious.
ex: They argued about trivial things like who forgot to wash the dishes.
nat: The mistake was trivial and did not affect the results.

mis.bad: It is a trivia problem.
mis.good: It is a trivial problem.
mis.why: Trivial is the adjective; trivia is a noun for small facts.

def: Not willing to change, or hard and not able to bend.
ex: The company has rigid rules about working hours and clothing.
nat: He was rigid in his thinking and refused to listen.

mis.bad: The rules are very rigorous and rigid at the same time.
mis.good: The rules are very rigid.
mis.why: Rigorous means very careful and exact; rigid means not flexible.

def: Done or chosen without a plan or pattern.
ex: The winner was chosen at random from over a thousand entries.
nat: A random stranger gave me directions to the station.

mis.bad: The winner was chosen in random.
mis.good: The winner was chosen at random.
mis.why: The fixed expression is "at random".

def: Very clear and detailed in your mind, or very bright.
ex: I have vivid memories of my first day at school.
nat: The painter used vivid colors to show the sunset.

mis.bad: I have a vivid memories of the trip.
mis.good: I have vivid memories of the trip.
mis.why: "A" cannot be used before a plural noun.

def: On purpose, not by accident.
ex: He deliberately ignored my message because he was angry with me.
nat: The sentence was deliberately written in simple words.

mis.bad: He did that of deliberately.
mis.good: He did that deliberately.
mis.why: Use the adverb deliberately without "of".

def: All the time, or very often.
ex: She is constantly checking her phone, even during meals with her family.
nat: Technology is constantly changing, so we must keep learning.

mis.bad: He constantly is complaining about work.
mis.good: He is constantly complaining about work.
mis.why: Place the adverb after "is" with a continuous verb.

def: Used to introduce more exact details about something you just mentioned.
ex: Only one thing worries me, namely the high cost of the project.
nat: The course covers two main areas, namely grammar and vocabulary.

mis.bad: I like two fruits, namely: apples and bananas.
mis.good: I like two fruits, namely apples and bananas.
mis.why: No colon after namely.

def: At an earlier time.
ex: She previously worked for a bank before she joined our company.
nat: The meeting, previously scheduled for Monday, will now be on Wednesday.

mis.bad: She worked previously for a bank in the 2010.
mis.good: She previously worked for a bank in 2010.
mis.why: Years take "in 2010", without "the".

def: Used to say that something is only what you say and no more.
ex: It was not a plan; it was merely an idea we discussed.
nat: I am not criticizing you; I merely want to understand.

mis.bad: He merely only wanted to help.
mis.good: He merely wanted to help.
mis.why: Merely and only mean the same; do not use both.

def: As you would expect, or in a way that is not forced.
ex: Naturally, I was upset when I heard that the trip was canceled.
nat: She speaks English naturally, as if it were her first language.

mis.bad: The nature of the problem is naturally.
mis.good: The problem is natural.
mis.why: Naturally is an adverb; use the adjective natural after "is".

def: Used to say that something appears to be true but may not be.
ex: Seemingly, the company has no plans to hire new staff this year.
nat: He gave a seemingly simple answer to a very hard question.

mis.bad: It seemingly that he is happy.
mis.good: Seemingly, he is happy.
mis.why: Seemingly is an adverb and cannot replace "it seems that".

def: Without any doubt.
ex: I will definitely come to your party on Saturday night.
nat: That was definitely the best pizza I have ever eaten.

mis.bad: I will definitly come to your party.
mis.good: I will definitely come to your party.
mis.why: The spelling is definitely, with "-ite".

def: Completely, with no limits.
ex: You are absolutely right; I made a mistake in the calculation.
nat: The food was absolutely delicious, and the service was perfect.

mis.bad: The food was absolutely good.
mis.good: The food was really good.
mis.why: Absolutely combines with strong adjectives (delicious, perfect), not with plain ones like good.

def: To a greater degree than usual.
ex: The traffic was particularly bad this morning because of the rain.
nat: I am not particularly interested in sports, but I like walking.

mis.bad: I am particular interested in history.
mis.good: I am particularly interested in history.
mis.why: Use the adverb particularly before an adjective.

def: Completely, in every way.
ex: The building was entirely destroyed by the fire last winter.
nat: I do not entirely agree with what you said.

mis.bad: The project is entire different now.
mis.good: The project is entirely different now.
mis.why: Use the adverb entirely before an adjective.

def: As a result.
ex: The factory closed; consequently, hundreds of people lost their jobs.
nat: She did not study; consequently, she failed the exam.

mis.bad: He was late, consequently of the traffic.
mis.good: He was late because of the traffic.
mis.why: Consequently introduces a result, not a cause; use "because of".

def: Used to add another point to what you have just said.
ex: The plan is too expensive; furthermore, it will take too long.
nat: The hotel is cheap; furthermore, it is close to the beach.

mis.bad: Furthermore, but it is also cheap.
mis.good: Furthermore, it is also cheap.
mis.why: Do not combine furthermore with "but".

def: A situation in which you must choose between two difficult options.
ex: She faced a dilemma when two companies offered her a job on the same day.
nat: I am in a dilemma about whether to move or stay.

mis.bad: I have a dilemma between to go or to stay.
mis.good: I have a dilemma about whether to go or stay.
mis.why: Use "dilemma about whether" or "dilemma over".

def: To succeed in dealing with a problem or a difficulty.
ex: He overcame his fear of speaking in public by practicing every day.
nat: We must overcome many obstacles before the project can start.

mis.bad: He overcame of his fear of flying.
mis.good: He overcame his fear of flying.
mis.why: Overcome is transitive; no "of".

def: To improve the quality or value of something.
ex: New software can enhance the quality of old photographs very quickly.
nat: Good lighting enhances the look of any room.

mis.bad: Reading can enhance to your vocabulary.
mis.good: Reading can enhance your vocabulary.
mis.why: Enhance is transitive; no "to".

def: Something that blocks your way or makes it difficult to achieve something.
ex: Lack of money is the biggest obstacle to starting a new business.
nat: A fallen tree was an obstacle on the road.

mis.bad: The biggest obstacle for success is fear.
mis.good: The biggest obstacle to success is fear.
mis.why: Use "obstacle to".

def: To make something start or happen suddenly.
ex: The news triggered a wave of protests in several cities across the country.
nat: Certain foods can trigger headaches in some people.

mis.bad: The smoke triggered to the alarm.
mis.good: The smoke triggered the alarm.
mis.why: Trigger is transitive; no "to".

def: To help something develop over time.
ex: The program aims to foster creativity among young students in rural schools.
nat: Good managers foster trust within their teams.

mis.bad: The teacher fostered to the students' creativity.
mis.good: The teacher fostered the students' creativity.
mis.why: Foster is transitive; no "to".

def: To experience a change or something difficult or unpleasant.
ex: The city has undergone major changes over the last twenty years.
nat: She will undergo surgery on her knee next month.

mis.bad: The city has undergoed many changes.
mis.good: The city has undergone many changes.
mis.why: The past participle of undergo is undergone.

def: To publicly support an idea or plan.
ex: The group advocates a ban on plastic bags in all supermarkets.
nat: Many doctors advocate regular exercise for people of all ages.

mis.bad: The group advocates for to ban plastic.
mis.good: The group advocates a ban on plastic.
mis.why: Advocate takes a noun object directly, or "for" in some uses, but not "for to".

def: A public disagreement about something that many people have strong opinions about.
ex: The new tax caused a lot of controversy among local business owners.
nat: There is some controversy about the results of the study.

mis.bad: There is a controversy of the new law.
mis.good: There is controversy over the new law.
mis.why: Use "controversy over" or "about".

def: To make something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is.
ex: He exaggerated the story so much that nobody believed him anymore.
nat: I am not exaggerating when I say the line was two hours long.

mis.bad: He always exaggerates of everything.
mis.good: He always exaggerates everything.
mis.why: Exaggerate is transitive; no "of".

def: To fail to notice something, or to choose not to react to it.
ex: I overlooked a small mistake in the contract, and it cost us money.
nat: We cannot overlook the fact that the project is already late.

mis.bad: I overlooked of the problem.
mis.good: I overlooked the problem.
mis.why: Overlook is transitive; no "of".

def: To show or prove that a decision or action is reasonable.
ex: How can you justify spending so much money on a single pair of shoes?
nat: Nothing can justify violence against innocent people.

mis.bad: I need to justify to my boss the expense.
mis.good: I need to justify the expense to my boss.
mis.why: Justify takes the thing directly, then "to" the person.

def: To expect something and be ready for it.
ex: We anticipate that demand will double during the holiday season this year.
nat: Good managers anticipate problems before they become serious.

mis.bad: I anticipate to see you soon.
mis.good: I look forward to seeing you soon.
mis.why: Anticipate is not used like "look forward to"; it means to expect and prepare.

def: Existing as a natural and permanent part of something.
ex: There are risks inherent in every kind of investment you make.
nat: Curiosity is inherent in all small children.

mis.bad: Risk is inherent of every investment.
mis.good: Risk is inherent in every investment.
mis.why: Use "inherent in".

def: To get involved in a situation in a way that is not wanted.
ex: Please do not interfere in my private life; I can solve my own problems.
nat: Loud noise from the street interfered with my sleep.

mis.bad: He always interferes my work.
mis.good: He always interferes with my work.
mis.why: Use "interfere with" or "interfere in".

def: In a way that shows you do not really want to do something.
ex: She reluctantly agreed to help, even though she was very busy.
nat: He reluctantly accepted the offer after thinking about it for days.

mis.bad: She agreed reluctant to help me.
mis.good: She reluctantly agreed to help me.
mis.why: Use the adverb reluctantly before the verb.

def: To behave as if something is true when it is not.
ex: She pretended to be asleep so that she would not have to talk.
nat: Do not pretend that you did not see the message.

mis.bad: He pretended that he is sick.
mis.good: He pretended that he was sick.
mis.why: After a past verb like pretended, the next verb usually shifts to the past.

def: To feel pain or experience something bad.
ex: Many people suffer from back pain after sitting at a desk all day.
nat: The company suffered heavy losses during the economic crisis.

mis.bad: He suffers of headaches every week.
mis.good: He suffers from headaches every week.
mis.why: Use "suffer from".

def: Sometimes, but not often.
ex: I occasionally work from a café when I need a change of scenery.
nat: We occasionally meet for lunch, but not every week.

mis.bad: I occasional go to the cinema.
mis.good: I occasionally go to the cinema.
mis.why: Use the adverb occasionally before the verb.
